prompt: In `shop.yaml`, what makes a pod count as one of the Deployment's three copies?
hint: The pod is never listed by name anywhere.

choices.text: Its labels match the selector
choices.why: Right. The template stamps `app: shop` and the selector counts every pod that carries it.

choices.text: Its name begins with the Deployment's name
choices.why: Names are generated and never consulted for ownership; labels and owner references are.

choices.text: It runs the image named in the template
choices.why: Many unrelated pods can run the same image; the selector looks at labels only.

choices.text: It listens on the port given in `containerPort`
choices.why: That field documents a port and plays no part in ownership.

prompt: What does `containerPort: 8080` do in the Deployment?
hint: The shop would listen on 8080 without it.

choices.text: Opens port 8080 on the node
choices.why: Nothing in a Deployment opens a node's port; a NodePort Service does.

choices.text: Tells the shop which port to listen on
choices.why: The program chooses its port; the shop reads its own `PORT` setting.

choices.text: It documents the port the container listens on, and opens nothing
choices.why: Right. It informs readers and tools; the Service's `targetPort` is what sends traffic there.

choices.text: Publishes the shop to the internet
choices.why: The pods were unreachable from the laptop until a port-forward or a NodePort was added.

prompt: Ana changes the template's label to `app: store` and applies, leaving the selector at `app: shop`. What happens?
hint: The selector has to match the template.

choices.text: The Service follows the new label
choices.why: The Service selects `app: shop` too, and nothing rewrites it.

choices.text: The API server refuses the Deployment
choices.why: Right. A selector that does not match its own template is rejected before anything runs.

choices.text: Three new pods start, and the old three keep running
choices.why: That would need the object to be accepted first, and it is not.

choices.text: The pods are renamed to match
choices.why: Labels and names are separate; nothing renames a pod.

prompt: In the Service, `port: 80` is what clients use, and `___: 8080` says which port of the pod the traffic goes to.
hint: The field's name says where the traffic is aimed.

prompt: Which command opened a tunnel from the laptop's port 8081 to the shop?
hint: It stops when the command stops.

choices.text: `kubectl apply -f shop-nodeport.yaml`
choices.why: That opened 30080 on every node, which is not a tunnel and does not stop with a command.

choices.text: `kubectl rollout status deployment/shop`
choices.why: That only waits for the pods to become available.

choices.text: `kubectl port-forward service/shop 8081:80`
choices.why: Right: a tool for a person, carried through the API server and the kubelet.

choices.text: `kubectl get service shop`
choices.why: That lists the Service; it changes nothing.

prompt: `kubectl get service shop-public` showed `80:30080/TCP`. What does that mean?
hint: Two places where the Service answers.

choices.text: Port 80 inside the pod, 30080 on the laptop
choices.why: The pod listens on 8080, and the laptop's port was 8080 by the cluster's mapping.

choices.text: Port 80 on the Service's address, and 30080 on every node
choices.why: Right. A NodePort Service is also a ClusterIP one, with a port opened on each node.

choices.text: Requests on 80 are redirected to 30080 with an HTTP status
choices.why: Nothing answers with a redirect; the packets are rewritten in the kernel.

choices.text: Only the node running a pod listens on 30080
choices.why: Every node does; the requests arrived at the control-plane node, which runs none of the shop's pods.

prompt: Six requests went to `localhost:8080`. How many different pods answered them?
The shop's log showed the NodePort requests arriving `from 172.18.0.2`. Why not from the laptop's own address?
hint: Which node did the requests reach first, and does the pod run there?

choices.text: The laptop and the control-plane node share one address
choices.why: The node is a container with an address of its own on Docker's network.

choices.text: The shop logs the node it runs on, not the client
choices.why: The pods run on the workers, and the port-forward line shows a different source.

choices.text: The first node rewrote the source, then forwarded it
choices.why: Right. That lets the reply come back through the same node; lesson 17 shows the setting that keeps the original.

choices.text: Every request inside a cluster is proxied through etcd
choices.why: etcd stores objects; it carries no traffic at all.

prompt: Put in order what happened between `kubectl apply -f shop.yaml` and the first answer through the NodePort.
hint: Objects first, then pods, then a way in.
items: The API server stores the Deployment and the Service
Three pods are scheduled onto the workers
The pods become available and the rollout completes
A NodePort Service opens 30080 on every node
A request to the laptop's 8080 reaches one of the pods
trap: No request can be answered before a pod is available, and none can arrive from outside before the NodePort exists.
